chapter.name: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations
chapter.blurb: This chapter extends the real numbers by introducing i = sqrt(-1), so that equations such as x^2 + 1 = 0 gain solutions, and defines a complex number a + ib with its real and imaginary parts. It develops the algebra of complex numbers -- addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, powers of i and square roots of negative reals -- together with the modulus, the conjugate and the multiplicative inverse. It closes by picturing complex numbers as points of the Argand plane.

scope_in.item: Explain why x^2 + 1 = 0 has no real solution and why the real number system is extended using i = sqrt(-1), with i^2 = -1
Recognise a complex number a + ib (a, b real) and read off its real part Re z and imaginary part Im z
Use equality of complex numbers (equal real parts and equal imaginary parts) to find real unknowns
Add and subtract complex numbers; state the closure, commutative and associative laws, the additive identity 0 + i0 and the additive inverse -z
Multiply complex numbers using (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc); state the closure, commutative, associative and distributive laws and the multiplicative identity 1 + i0
Use the identities for (z1 + z2)^2, (z1 - z2)^2, (z1 + z2)^3, (z1 - z2)^3 and z1^2 - z2^2 to express powers and products in the form a + ib
Evaluate integer powers of i, positive and negative, using i^4k = 1, i^(4k+1) = i, i^(4k+2) = -1, i^(4k+3) = -i
Give the square roots of a negative real number, use sqrt(-a) = sqrt(a) i for a > 0, and know that sqrt(a) sqrt(b) = sqrt(ab) fails when a and b are both negative
Find the modulus |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and the conjugate a - ib of a complex number, and use the stated results on modulus and conjugate of products, quotients and sums
Find the multiplicative inverse of a non-zero complex number as (conjugate of z)/|z|^2, and divide complex numbers to reach the form a + ib
Represent a complex number x + iy as the point (x, y) of the Argand plane, name the real and imaginary axes, and read the modulus as distance from the origin
Locate the conjugate of z in the Argand plane as the mirror image of z in the real axis

concepts.name: Complex numbers: i, real and imaginary parts, equality
concepts.description: The need for i = sqrt(-1), the form a + ib, Re z and Im z, and equality of two complex numbers used to find real unknowns.
concepts.idea: No real number has square -1, so a new number i with i^2 = -1 is introduced. Every complex number is a + ib with a and b real.
concepts.rule: For z = a + ib, Re z = a and Im z = b (a real number, not ib). a + ib = c + id if a = c and b = d.
concepts.example: If 4x + i(3x - y) = 3 + i(-6), then 4x = 3 and 3x - y = -6, so x = 3/4 and y = 33/4.

concepts.name: The Argand plane
concepts.description: Representing x + iy as the point (x, y), the real and imaginary axes, modulus as distance from the origin, and the conjugate as a mirror image in the real axis.
concepts.idea: Each complex number x + iy is one point (x, y) of a plane, and each point is one complex number.
concepts.rule: The x-axis is the real axis (numbers a + i0) and the y-axis is the imaginary axis (numbers 0 + ib). |x + iy| is the distance of (x, y) from the origin. The conjugate is the point (x, -y).
concepts.example: -2 + 3i is the point (-2, 3); its conjugate -2 - 3i is the point (-2, -3), the mirror image in the real axis.

questions.q: In the Argand plane P represents z = 3 + 4i and Q represents the conjugate of z. Find the coordinates of P and Q, the distance of each from the origin, and the length PQ.
questions.a: P is (3, 4). The conjugate is 3 - 4i, so Q is (3, -4). OP = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 and OQ = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. P and Q have the same x-coordinate, so PQ = 4 - (-4) = 8.
s: Gives P(3, 4) and Q(3, -4)
Finds OP = OQ = 5
Finds PQ = 8

In the Argand plane F(1, -2) represents the complex number z. Let Q represent the conjugate of z and R represent z + (conjugate of z). Find Q and R, explain why R lies on the real axis, and find the distances of F and Q from the origin.
questions.a: z = 1 - 2i, so its conjugate is 1 + 2i and Q is (1, 2), the mirror image of F in the real axis. z + conjugate = (1 + 1) + i(-2 + 2) = 2 + 0i, so R is (2, 0). R lies on the real axis because the imaginary parts -2 and 2 cancel, leaving a number of the form a + i0. OF = sqrt(1 + 4) = sqrt(5) and OQ = sqrt(1 + 4) = sqrt(5).
s: Finds Q(1, 2) as the point of the conjugate 1 + 2i
Finds R(2, 0) and explains the imaginary parts cancel, giving the form a + i0
Finds OF = OQ = sqrt(5)

questions.q: Dev says: 'The conjugate of z is found by reflecting its point in the y-axis, so the conjugate of 2 + 3i is plotted at (-2, 3).' Evaluate his statement.
questions.a: He is wrong. The conjugate of 2 + 3i is 2 - 3i, plotted at (2, -3). The conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part only, so its point (x, -y) is the mirror image of (x, y) in the real axis (x-axis), not the y-axis. He changed the sign of the real part.
s: Gives the correct point (2, -3) for the conjugate 2 - 3i
Identifies the error: reflection is in the real axis (sign of imaginary part changes), not the y-axis

questions.q: Construct a complex number z with a negative real part, lying on neither axis of the Argand plane, whose point is at distance 5 from the origin. Give the points representing z and its conjugate and verify the distance.
questions.a: For example z = -3 + 4i, represented by (-3, 4). Its conjugate is -3 - 4i, represented by (-3, -4). Distance of (-3, 4) from the origin = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5. Neither coordinate is 0, so the point lies on neither axis. (Any correct choice, such as -4 + 3i or -3 - 4i, earns full marks.)
s: Gives a valid z with negative real part and non-zero imaginary part
States the points of z and of its conjugate correctly
Verifies the distance sqrt(x^2 + y^2) = 5
